title: The XG Files: Falcon C2 Flying Under The (Browser) Radar
text: Antino is written in Rust and dates back to at least Oct. 6, 2025, based on the compilation timestamp of the earliest known sample. The name originates from the filename of the oldest known sample antino-client.exe, along with PDB strings in the binary, such as antino_client.pdb.

title: The XG Files: Falcon C2 Flying Under The (Browser) Radar
text: Antino uses passive execution to establish persistence in the Windows Registry. It first copies itself to the hard-coded directory %LOCALAPPDATA%\Windows GatherOSStateKit\tmp<8 char>.exe and attempts to copy two DLLs, DllSafeCheck64.dll and slc.dll, from its current directory.

title: The XG Files: Falcon C2 Flying Under The (Browser) Radar
text: Antino executes the Microsoft Scripted Diagnostic Native Host utility (sdiagnhost.exe), which parses the diagnostic answer file. The first XML section highlighted in red defines the header, and the text that follows is the path required to load the Program Compatibility Wizard (PCW). The contents highlighted in purple are the answer file folder name. The contents highlighted in blue are the answer file filename. The PowerShell snippet highlighted in light magenta is ultimately executed in the context of sdiagnhost.exe and adds Antino to the Windows Registry Run key.

title: QUIC and Covert: Novel HTTP/3-Powered RATs Target Southeast Asian Governments
text: Multi-vector heuristic camouflage: KUKURAT employs a custom spoofing engine that generates synthetic, benign-looking network, registry and file activity. By manipulating the behavioral baseline of the endpoint, it can successfully obscure indicators of compromise within a vast volume of artificial noise.

title: QUIC and Covert: Novel HTTP/3-Powered RATs Target Southeast Asian Governments
text: KUKURAT introduces a unique heuristic camouflage engine capable of operating across three system axes: network, registry and files. The purpose of this engine is to generate dummy, legitimate-looking activity on the endpoint to camouflage the malware's actual operations. By mimicking normal operational behavior, the threat actor establishes a false baseline, which may significantly affect automated detection and other forensic efforts. The threat actor can toggle each method on or off via the C2 command set_obfuscation:

title: QUIC and Covert: Novel HTTP/3-Powered RATs Target Southeast Asian Governments
text: Registry manipulation mimicking browser activity: KUKURAT mimics legitimate Google Chrome browser behavior by writing random data to the registry path HKCU\Software\Google\Chrome\BrowserCrashRecovery, reading the data back, and then deleting the key. It then opens and enumerates the HKCU\Software\Google\Update\ClientState registry key. The purpose of this sequence is to make the agent's registry operation appear like Chrome crash recovery.

text: On one occasion, we observed the threat actor deploying this watchdog component into the C:\ProgramData\Cyvera\Ransomware\ directory path. This folder structure was historically associated with Cortex XDR, demonstrating the threat actor’s attempt to lower suspicion by hiding within security-product directory structures.

title: QUIC and Covert: Novel HTTP/3-Powered RATs Target Southeast Asian Governments
text: The threat actor’s most notable method for network propagation involves the manipulation of domain log-on scripts, a stealthy persistence mechanism used to execute code across the environment. In addition, they use well-known tools and remote management protocols such as PsExec, Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) and Windows Remote Management (WinRM).
